content_blocks.text: Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Sections 15 to 17 introduce a couple of new notices: planned procurement notices and preliminary market engagement notices.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Planned procurement notice
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: A planned procurement notice isn’t mandatory. It operates to alert the market to a particular procurement and to reduce the time limit for tenders to 10 days in certain qualifying circumstances. It cannot be used to commence a procurement.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on Planned Procurement Notices is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Preliminary market engagement notice
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: A preliminary market engagement notice is published to communicate to suppliers that the authority either intends to carry out a market engagement exercise or has carried out a market engagement exercise.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Where preliminary market engagement has been used, it is mandatory to publish one ahead of publishing the tender notice (unless the authority can justify a decision not to publish one).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Preliminary market engagement guidance makes it clear that the expectation is that non-publication will be appropriate in only limited circumstances, for example where there are national security issues or time critical factors.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on Preliminary Market Engagement Notices is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Division into Lots
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Similarly, section 18 imposes a duty on authorities to consider division into lots. This duty should also be read in the light of the new express obligation at section 12 to consider and attempt to reduce barriers to small and medium-sized enterprises (SME) participation in a procurement.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on use of Lots is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Preliminary steps (sections 15-18)

content_blocks.text: Competitive award (sections 19-40)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: MEAT to MAT and assessment of tenders
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 19(1) sets out the core obligation to award a contract to the supplier that submits the most advantageous tender (MAT) and confirms that it best satisfies the award criteria in accordance with the published assessment methodology and weightings. The new regime shifts from the existing most economically advantageous tender (MEAT) and will allow contracts to be awarded to the most advantageous tender, widening the possibility of award to contracts that best further general procurement policies, including social value. This flexibility is set within a general requirement to set criteria in a way which is proportionate to the contract.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on assessing competitive tenders is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Competitive tendering procedures
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 20 creates one concept of a "competitive tendering procedure" - which may be either:
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: A single-stage open procedure; or
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Any other competitive procedure that the authority considers appropriate (introducing freedom to design a procedure). This may contain deselection phases and, in a new flexibility, may provide for the refinement of award criteria in accordance with the Act (a competitive flexible procedure).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: This represents significant change to procurement procedures under the old regime and will allow greater flexibility to design more bespoke procedures within a broad framework.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Whatever procedure is adopted, it must be proportionate to the nature, complexity, and cost of the contract (section 20(3)).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Sections 21(5) and (6) impose an express duty on authorities, when publishing a tender notice, to ensure that details of the requirements are sufficiently clear and specific as to allow suppliers to prepare their tenders.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on competitive tendering procedures is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Guidance on time frames is here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Conditions of participation (selection criteria)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 22 deals with what we currently refer to as selection criteria, and what are referred to in the Act as conditions of participation .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: These conditions are aimed at ensuring suppliers have the legal and financial capacity and the technical ability to perform the contract.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 22(4) gives the authority to discretion to set the conditions, but these must be proportionate to the cost, nature and complexity of the contract. Note that “economic and financial standing” becomes “legal and financial capacity”, while “technical and professional ability” becomes “technical ability”.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 22(3) prevents authorities from requiring the submission of annual accounts or requiring insurances prior to the award of the contract, as part of the conditions of participation.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 22(4) prohibits any condition of participation that requires a supplier to have been awarded a particular contract previously, or to have qualifications without accepting equivalents, or that breaks the rules on technical specifications in section 56.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: The majority of a supplier's standard selection information will be uploaded to the Supplier Information Service (part of the Central Digital Platform) (instead of via the CCS Standard Selection Questionnaire, as previously).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on conditions of participation is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Award criteria – link to subject matter of the contract
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: The requirement that the award criteria be linked to the subject matter of the contract is retained generally. Section 23(5) makes it clear that, as now, staff experience and qualifications are linked to the subject matter where this makes a material difference to the quality of provision under the contract.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Refinement of award criteria
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 24 introduces a useful flexibility to refine award criteria and relative weightings during a procurement, provided that:
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: It's not an open procedure
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: The ITT document hasn’t been issued
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: There are no suppliers who have been excluded from the process who would have been able to progress had the refinement been in place at the time of their exclusion
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: The procurement documents must have reserved the right to make this refinement, and making these changes triggers an obligation to republish the tender notice/documents.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: A refinement isn’t permitted if, had it been made earlier, it would have allowed one or more suppliers (that didn’t progress beyond an earlier round or selection process) to have done so.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Excluding suppliers
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: New terminology is introduced - excluded suppliers (excluded on a mandatory ground) and excludable suppliers (excludable on a discretionary ground).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Excluded suppliers must be excluded from the procurement, while the authority may exclude excludable suppliers. The mandatory grounds are set out in full in Schedule 6 and the discretionary grounds in Schedule 7.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: A supplier can also be excluded and/or excludable if an associated supplier is itself excluded and/or excludable. An associated supplier is a supplier the tenderer is relying on to deliver the contract. The tenderer must be given an opportunity to replace an associated person prior to any exclusion (section 26(3)).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: A similar regime applies in relation to sub-contractors (see section 28).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: In addition to the mandatory and discretionary grounds set out in schedules 6 and 7, there are extra sections permitting exclusions for improper behaviour (section 30), or where the supplier is a threat to national security (section 29).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Any exclusion triggers a duty on the authority to refer the exclusion to the Procurement Review Unit.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on excluding suppliers is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Modifying a procurement
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Section 31 contains a helpful flexibility allowing a contracting authority to modify the terms of a procurement provided the tender deadline hasn’t passed (for an open process) or the request to participate period hasn’t ended (for a competitive flexible procedure).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Any modification of this sort triggers an obligation to re-publish the tender notice.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: If that modification isn’t "substantial", a competitive flexible process may be modified ahead of the tender deadline (not only during the participation period). It will not be necessary to republish the tender notice, but all suppliers must be notified.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: "Substantial" modifications to the tender process are those which would have the potential to change the field of suppliers who would or wouldn’t have been interested in taking part. Such substantial modifications to the procedure aren’t permitted. In both cases, consideration must be given to amending timelines and deadlines where appropriate.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Dynamic markets
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Sections 34-40 set out the basics for how dynamic markets (the new terms for a dynamic purchasing system) are to be set up and how contracts can be called off from these. It also confirms that a fee may be charged to suppliers award a contract under a dynamic market, which may make this route more attractive for authorities who will be able to cover the costs of administering the system.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on dynamic markets is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Competitive award (sections 19-40)

content_blocks.text: Direct award (sections 41-44)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The Act also sets out several limited scenarios for the direct awards of contracts with no competition.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Section 41 covers direct award in special cases, referring to the direct award justifications in Schedule 5 and the requirement to publish a transparency notice (ie a notice before awarding the contract confirming the intention to direct award a contract) under section 44.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The requirement to publish a contract details notice to notify the market once the contract has been awarded remains.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Some of the situations listed in Schedule 5 are new and others are based on those in the previous rules:
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The contract is for the production of a prototype or otherwise novel goods/services (NEW)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Only a single supplier can supply the requirement
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The procurement is for additional/repeated goods, services or works
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The contract is for a commodity (eg raw materials where tendering in the usual way would not be appropriate) (NEW)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: In the context of insolvency proceedings, the direct award to a particular supplier will obtain advantageous terms to the authority
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The contract is for strictly necessary goods, services or works and cannot be awarded following a competitive tendering procedure for reasons of unforeseen extreme and unavoidable urgency
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: The contract is for a light touch service which is a user choice service intended to allow direct awards for, eg personal social care (note no transparency notice is required under this particular ground)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Defence contracts where certain conditions are met
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Section 42 also allows direct awards where regulations are made by the government permitting this in order to protect life. This takes the decision about whether to direct award in these cases out of the hands of contracting authorities and as such no transparency notices are required here.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Section 43 allows a procurement to switch to direct award where no suitable tenders have been received and helpful sets out a definition of suitable. This mirrors Regulation 32(2)(a), although a new element under the Act is that a transparency notice must be published in this situation.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Planned direct awards of contracts fall within scope of the new section 93 obligation (applying to authorities intending to spend £100+ million in a financial year) requiring a pipeline notice to be published setting out details of all proposed contracts valued at over £2 million (including those contracts the authority expects to direct award).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on direct award is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Direct award (sections 41-44)

content_blocks.text: Frameworks (sections 45-49)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: There will continue to be closed frameworks of a 4-year duration which operate as frameworks do currently.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: In addition, there’s a new concept of an open framework , a series of frameworks on similar terms which can operate for a maximum of up to eight years and allow new suppliers to join during the lifetime of the framework.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: Section 49(1) defines an open framework as one that provides for the award of successive frameworks on essentially the same terms (i.e. the same framework can essentially roll over successively) provided it is re-opened to new suppliers (section 49(2)).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: The approach to admitting new suppliers to the framework will vary depending on whether there is any stated maximum number of permissible suppliers (if there is, there will need to be a new competition on the re-opening of the framework, with the possibility that an existing supplier may no longer score highly enough to keep its place). Where there is no limit, it is possible to elect to "roll over" existing suppliers and to assess new suppliers for addition.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: There is usually a maximum term limit of 8 years for an open framework scheme. However, this may be extended in certain specific circumstances if the authority is satisfied that nature of the contract requires it and can publish such a justification.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: If the terms are to change, then it cannot be an open framework (i.e. successive on the same terms) and a new competitive tendering process must be conducted.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: This new flexibility is helpful as will make it easier to renew frameworks where there’s no material change to the scope or terms/conditions, without having to run a full new tender process.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: Section 45(7) states any fees are to be charged as a % of contract value each time a contract is awarded to the supplier.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on framework agreements is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
Frameworks (sections 45-49)

content_blocks.text: After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Contract award notices and assessment summaries
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Section 50 requires contracting authorities to publish a Contract Award Notice notifying the market that it intends to enter into a contract (i.e. before awarding the contract). Note the terminology change, this is not a “CAN” as we currently understand it, that’s known under the Act as a Contract Details Notice.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Sending the contract award notice commences the standstill period and announces that the authority has sent assessment summaries of feedback to the successful and unsuccessful tenderers.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: The detail of content required in an assessment summary is set out in the Procurement Regulations 2024. The language around relative advantages and characteristics has disappeared, and instead authorities will simply be required to give feedback as to the reasons for scores on the recipient’s bid and on the winning bid. This should make the drafting significantly easier than is the case for standstill letters currently.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on Assessment Summaries is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Standstill period
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Section 51 mandates a standstill period of 8 working days, beginning with the day on which the Contract Award Notice is published.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: There’s no requirement to hold a standstill period for
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Light touch contracts
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Contracts called off under a framework or dynamic market
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Where a direct award is made on the urgency or protect life ground
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: However this can be a useful risk mitigation approach.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on Contract Award Notices and Standstill is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Our Procurement Act 2023 standstill calculator is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Key performance indicators
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Section 52 requires, where a contract is valued at over £5 million , at least three key performance indicators (KPIs) must be published via a Contract Performance Notice (and reported against at least every 12 months (section 71(2)).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: This is not required if the authority considers that performance of the contract cannot sensibly be assessed by reference to KPIs.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: The obligation doesn’t apply to framework agreements, utilities contracts, concession contracts, or light touch contracts.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Where more than three KPIs are set, the authority must publish all of them (this requirement will usually be satisfied by way of the obligation to publish a copy of contracts valued at over £5 million).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: The Contract Details Notice (see below) must set out which three KPIs the authority considers most material to the contract (and to make a note if it is expected that this may change over the lifetime of the contract).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: The Contract Performance Notice must report on the three KPIs the authority considers most material to the performance of the contract as at the date the notice is published. The Act prescribes the reporting matrix for assessing performance, as follows
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on key performance indicators is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Contract details notices and publication of contracts
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Section 53 requires a notice similar to contract award notice under the previous procurement rules. Under the Act, this is now referred to as a Contract Details Notice.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: It must be published within 30 days of the date of contract signature (or 120 days if it is a light touch contract).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: For contracts valued at over £5 million , a copy of the contract must be published within 90 days of the date of contract signature (or 180 days for light touch contracts).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on Contract Details Notices is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
After award; assessment summaries, standstill, and notices (sections 50-53)

content_blocks.text: General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Time limits
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Although there is flexibility on a competitive flexible procedure can be designed, section 54 sets out certain minimum time limits for the participation period (the selection stage) and the tendering period (the award stage).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Please see our Procurement Act 2023 Timescale Tracker for further information, available here [insert link].
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: The minimum timescales for what we currently refer to as an accelerated restricted process appear to remain unchanged. There are no minimum timescales for light touch contracts but, in setting time limits, regard must be had to the general principles set out in section 54(1).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Where a qualifying planned procurement notice has been published in advance, there’s flexibility to reduce the tender period to a minimum of 10 days, subject to the general rules on ensuring proportionality of timescales.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Government guidance on setting time limits is available here .
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Abandoning a procurement
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Section 55 introduces a new requirement to publish a procurement termination notice in circumstances where a procurement is abandoned.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Technical specifications

content_blocks.text: The Act takes the same broad position as previous regime around the requirement to accept equivalents. Authorities also need to note the new obligation at section 56 that the specification must be sufficiently developed and clear that suppliers can tender to it, prior to publishing the tender notice. This was implicit in the previous regime, but the Act makes this an express requirement.

content_blocks.text: Excluding suppliers/debarment
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Section 59 requires a contracting authority which has excluded a supplier to give notice to an appropriate authority within 30 days of this exclusion.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Under section 60, the appropriate authority may then decide to investigate whether the supplier is indeed an excluded supplier (mandatory exclusions) or an excludable supplier (discretionary exclusions). Authorities and suppliers are required to cooperate.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Section 62 then states that this report is then used by the Secretary of State to determine whether the supplier should be added to a debarment list under section 62 (notice and an explanation must be provided to the supplier). The length of the debarment is decided by the Secretary of State.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Section 63 allows a supplier to apply to the High Court for an injunction to prevent the Secretary of State adding it to the debarment list until the court has made a ruling on the question. The court, in making that decision, will consider the public interest and the likely impact of the debarment on the supplier (together with any other relevant factors).
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Section 64 states that a supplier may apply to be removed from the debarment list, but the Secretary of State must only consider this if a material change in circumstances is evidenced.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Section 65 gives suppliers a right to appeal to the High Court against either their inclusion on the debarment list or against the length of their debarment.

content_blocks.text: Exclusion for Past performance
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures

content_blocks.text: This ground is expanded to also include a situation where a supplier has failed to remedy a breach following the authority having exercised a contractual right to require it to do so. This represents a widening of the ground. Poor performance is rarely dealt with via termination/a court order, but, rather contractually as between the parties. These latter measures may now come within scope of this ground.
heading_path: Award of public contracts and procedures
General provision about award and procedures (sections 54-66)

content_blocks.text: Schedule 7(12)(3) sets out this discretionary ground for failure to remedy. This applies where the supplier hasn’t performed the contract to the authority’s satisfaction and has failed to remedy upon being given the opportunity to do so. The challenge for suppliers here is that the ground gives the authority a good deal of discretion and doesn’t carve out situations where the failure to remedy is outside the supplier’s control. That said, the authority will need to act in accordance with the procurement objectives, which will include being proportionate and fair. Where a performance failure is more serious, and hasn’t been remedied, this must be assessed and published within 30 days of the relevant failure (note this does not apply to light touch regime contracts).

content_blocks.text: The central digital platform referenced in the guidance comprises an enhanced version of Find a Tender (FTS), providing the new procurement notices, and a new Supplier Information Service (SIS). Access the central digital platform, which will be supported by a single place of registration for both parts of the service, and for both FTS and SIS, using the same account.
